subject: Behavioral Economics
title: The Conjunction Fallacy
description: A quick, practical guide to The Conjunction Fallacy.

hook.text: Linda is 31, outspoken, and studied philosophy. Is she a bank teller or a feminist bank teller?

buildup.text: 85% chose 'feminist bank teller.' But that's two conditions at once, which is always less probable.

discovery.text: The conjunction fallacy: adding detail makes a story feel truer even though it's statistically less likely.

twist.text: Our brains judge by narrative fit, not probability. A good story beats cold math every time.

climax.text: More specific doesn't mean more probable. Every added condition only narrows the odds.

quiz.question: Why is 'feminist bank teller' less likely than 'bank teller'?
options: Two conditions combined are always less probable than one alone

details.summary: The conjunction fallacy occurs when people judge a specific combination of events as more likely than either event alone, violating basic probability. The famous Linda problem showed that people rated Linda as more likely to be a feminist bank teller than just a bank teller.
details.whyItMatters: The conjunction fallacy reveals that intuitive probability judgments are based on narrative coherence rather than statistical logic.
takeaways: Adding specific details makes events seem more likely, not less
The Linda problem demonstrates the fallacy with remarkable consistency
Narrative coherence overrides statistical logic in probability judgments

faq.question: What is the Linda problem?
faq.answer: Linda is described as a socially conscious philosophy graduate. People rate 'Linda is a bank teller and a feminist' as more probable than 'Linda is a bank teller.' But logically, the combination can never be more probable than either element alone.

faq.question: Why do detailed scenarios seem more probable than simple ones?
faq.answer: Representativeness heuristic: detailed scenarios are easier to imagine and fit coherent narratives. A story with consistent details feels true. The brain evaluates plausibility through storytelling rather than probability calculation.
